title: Von dem Tode des Hühnchens
titleEn: The Death of the Little Hen
part: The Death of the Little Hen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 80. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, theilen, Thiere, Noth, todt/todten).
about: KHM 80, a chain tale that starts as a joke and then does not stop. A little hen chokes on a nut-kernel she meant to eat alone; the little cock’s errand for water runs him from well to bride to willow and back, and arrives too late; and the funeral procession that follows drowns, burns out and collapses by stages until nothing in the tale is left alive. Grimm keeps the whole of it in diminutives — Hühnchen, Hähnchen, Kränzlein, Pferdchen — so that the surface stays small and light while the tale kills everything it names.

sentences.t: Auf eine Zeit gieng das Hühnchen mit dem Hähnchen in den Nußberg, und sie machten mit einander aus wer einen Nußkern fände, sollte ihn mit dem andern theilen.
sentences.l: On a time the little hen went with the little cock into the nut-hill, and they settled with each other that whoever found a nut-kernel should share it with the other.
sentences.i: Once upon a time the little hen went with the little cock to the nut-hill, and they agreed between them that whoever found a nut-kernel should share it with the other.
sentences.n: “auf eine Zeit” is an old way of saying “once”. ausmachen (to agree, to settle) is separable: “machten… aus”. fände is subjunctive, holding the agreement open as a condition. Hühnchen and Hähnchen are the diminutives of Huhn and Hahn — the small register the whole tale is told in.

sentences.t: Nun fand das Hühnchen eine große große Nuß, sagte aber nichts davon und wollte den Kern allein essen.
sentences.l: Now the little hen found a great, great nut, but said nothing of it and wanted to eat the kernel alone.
sentences.n: German will not put a pronoun after a preposition when it stands for a thing; it fuses da- onto the preposition instead — davon here, later daran, dafür, drüber.

sentences.t: Der Kern war aber so dick, daß es ihn nicht hinunter schlucken konnte, und er ihm im Hals stecken blieb, daß ihm angst wurde es müßte ersticken.
sentences.l: But the kernel was so thick that it could not swallow it down, and it stuck fast in its throat, so that it grew afraid it would choke.
sentences.i: But the kernel was so thick that she could not swallow it down, and it stuck fast in her throat, so that she grew afraid she would choke.
sentences.n: The hen is grammatically neuter — das Hühnchen — so German calls her “it” throughout; English has to choose, and the idiomatic line says “she”. “ihm angst wurde” is the impersonal construction with the frightened one in the dative. müßte is subjunctive: what she feared, not what had happened.

sentences.t: Da schrie das Hühnchen „Hähnchen, ich bitte dich lauf, was du kannst, und hol mir Wasser, sonst erstick ich.“
sentences.l: Then the little hen cried “little cock, I beg you, run what you can, and fetch me water, or else I choke.”
sentences.i: Then the little hen cried: “Little cock, I beg you, run as fast as you can and fetch me water, or I shall choke.”
sentences.n: “lauf, was du kannst” = run for all you are worth.

sentences.t: Das Hähnchen lief, was es konnte, zum Brunnen, und sprach „Born, du sollst mir Wasser geben; das Hühnchen liegt auf dem Nußberg, hat einen großen Nußkern geschluckt und will ersticken.“
sentences.l: The little cock ran what it could to the well, and spoke “spring, you shall give me water; the little hen lies on the nut-hill, has swallowed a great nut-kernel and is going to choke.”
sentences.i: The little cock ran as fast as he could to the well and said: “Spring, you must give me water. The little hen lies on the nut-hill; she has swallowed a great nut-kernel and is choking.”
sentences.n: Born is the older, more poetic word for Brunnen, a spring or well — the tale uses both within a single sentence. wollen here is not “to want” but “to be on the point of”: “will ersticken” = is about to choke.

sentences.t: Der Brunnen antwortete „lauf erst hin zur Braut, und laß dir rothe Seide geben.“
sentences.l: The well answered “run first to the bride, and have red silk given to you.”
sentences.i: The well answered: “Run first to the bride, and get her to give you red silk.”
sentences.n: “laß dir geben” = have it given to you, get it from her. The chain has started: each helper sends the cock one step further from the choking hen.

sentences.t: Das Hähnchen lief zur Braut, „Braut, du sollst mir rothe Seide geben: rothe Seide will ich dem Brunnen geben, der Brunnen soll mir Wasser geben, das Wasser will ich dem Hühnchen bringen, das liegt auf dem Nußberg, hat einen großen Nußkern geschluckt und will daran ersticken.“
sentences.l: The little cock ran to the bride: “bride, you shall give me red silk: red silk I will give to the well, the well shall give me water, the water I will bring to the little hen, which lies on the nut-hill, has swallowed a great nut-kernel and is going to choke on it.”
sentences.i: The little cock ran to the bride: “Bride, you must give me red silk. The red silk I will give to the well, the well shall give me water, the water I will bring to the little hen, who lies on the nut-hill; she has swallowed a great nut-kernel and is choking on it.”
sentences.n: The engine of a chain tale: every errand recites the whole chain back from the newest link to the dying hen. Grimm sets it out in full only this once and leaves the rest to be understood.

sentences.t: Die Braut antwortete „lauf erst und hol mir mein Kränzlein, das blieb an einer Weide hängen.“
sentences.l: The bride answered “run first and fetch me my little wreath — it stayed hanging on a willow.”
sentences.i: The bride answered: “Run first and fetch me my little wreath; it was left hanging on a willow.”
sentences.n: A Kränzlein is the bridal wreath. “hängen bleiben” = to be left hanging, to catch on something.

sentences.t: Da lief das Hähnchen zur Weide und zog das Kränzlein von dem Ast und brachte es der Braut, und die Braut gab ihm rothe Seide dafür, die brachte es dem Brunnen, der gab ihm Wasser dafür.
sentences.l: Then the little cock ran to the willow and drew the little wreath from the branch and brought it to the bride, and the bride gave it red silk for it; that it brought to the well, and that one gave it water for it.
sentences.i: Then the little cock ran to the willow and drew the wreath off the branch and brought it to the bride, and the bride gave him red silk for it; that he brought to the well, and the well gave him water for it.
sentences.n: Two pointing demonstratives carry the sentence along — “die brachte es dem Brunnen, der gab ihm Wasser”, “that he brought to the well, and that one gave him water”. The whole chain is undone in a single breath, and it is still too late.

sentences.t: Da brachte das Hähnchen das Wasser zum Hühnchen, wie es aber hinkam, war dieweil das Hühnchen erstickt, und lag da todt und regte sich nicht.
sentences.l: Then the little cock brought the water to the little hen; but as it got there, in the meantime the little hen had choked, and lay there dead and did not stir.
sentences.i: Then the little cock brought the water to the little hen; but by the time he got there, the little hen had choked in the meanwhile, and lay there dead and did not stir.
sentences.n: dieweil is an old word for “meanwhile” (modern derweil); the same word, worn down, is the modern weil, “because”.

sentences.t: Da war das Hähnchen so traurig, daß es laut schrie, und kamen alle Thiere und beklagten das Hühnchen; und sechs Mäuse bauten einen kleinen Wagen, das Hühnchen darin zum Grabe zu fahren; und als der Wagen fertig war, spannten sie sich davor, und das Hähnchen fuhr.
sentences.l: Then the little cock was so sad that it cried aloud, and there came all the animals and lamented the little hen; and six mice built a little cart, to carry the little hen in it to the grave; and when the cart was ready, they harnessed themselves before it, and the little cock drove.
sentences.i: Then the little cock was so sad that he cried aloud, and all the beasts came and mourned the little hen; and six mice built a little cart to carry her to the grave; and when the cart was ready they harnessed themselves in front of it, and the little cock drove.
sentences.n: “und kamen alle Thiere” runs straight on with its verb first and no es or da in front of it — part of the loose, breathless stringing of und that carries the whole second half of this tale. “sich davor spannen” = to harness oneself in front of it.

sentences.t: Auf dem Wege aber kam der Fuchs, „wo willst du hin, Hähnchen?“
sentences.l: But on the way came the fox: “where do you want to go, little cock?”
sentences.i: But on the way came the fox: “Where are you off to, little cock?”
sentences.n: “wo willst du hin” = where are you going — the verb of motion is simply left out after the modal, as German freely does.

sentences.t: „Ich will mein Hühnchen begraben.“
sentences.l: “I want to bury my little hen.”
sentences.i: “I am going to bury my little hen.”

sentences.t: „Darf ich mitfahren?“
sentences.l: “May I ride along?”

sentences.t:
„Ja, aber setz dich hinten auf den Wagen,
vorn könnens meine Pferdchen nicht vertragen.“
sentences.l:
“Yes, but seat yourself behind on the cart,
in front my little horses cannot bear it.”
sentences.i:
“Yes, but sit yourself at the back of the cart;
at the front my little horses could not bear it.”
sentences.n: The one rhymed couplet in the tale (Wagen / vertragen). könnens = können es. The little horses are the six mice.

sentences.t: Da setzte sich der Fuchs hinten auf, dann der Wolf, der Bär, der Hirsch, der Löwe und alle Thiere in dem Wald.
sentences.l: Then the fox seated himself behind, then the wolf, the bear, the stag, the lion and all the animals in the wood.
sentences.i: So the fox sat himself at the back, and then the wolf, the bear, the stag, the lion and all the beasts of the wood.
sentences.n: A German forest with a lion in it: the list of beasts is a formula, not a natural history.

sentences.t: So gieng die Fahrt fort, da kamen sie an einen Bach.
sentences.l: So the journey went on, and they came to a brook.

sentences.t: „Wie sollen wir nun hinüber?“ sagte das Hähnchen.
sentences.l: “How shall we get over now?” said the little cock.
sentences.n: hin- points away from the speaker, her- toward: hinüber over to the far side, herab down. The verb of motion drops out after the modal again.

sentences.t: Da lag ein Strohhalm am Bach, der sagte „ich will mich queer drüber legen, so könnt ihr über mich fahren.“
sentences.l: There lay a straw at the brook; it said “I will lay myself crosswise over it, then you can drive over me.”
sentences.i: A straw was lying by the brook, and it said: “I will lay myself across, and then you can drive over me.”
sentences.n: queer is the 1857 spelling of quer (crosswise). The straw and the coal that follow have a tale of their own in the collection, KHM 18 Strohhalm, Kohle und Bohne, where a straw likewise lays itself across water and a coal likewise perishes on it.

sentences.t: Wie aber die sechs Mäuse auf die Brücke kamen, rutschte der Strohhalm und fiel ins Wasser, und die sechs Mäuse fielen alle hinein und ertranken.
sentences.l: But when the six mice came onto the bridge, the straw slipped and fell into the water, and the six mice all fell in and drowned.
sentences.n: wie at the head of a clause is “when,” not “how”; it does this four times over. The straw is then called “die Brücke,” definite, as though it had always been one.

sentences.t: Da gieng die Noth von neuem an, und kam eine Kohle und sagte „ich bin groß genug, ich will mich darüber legen und ihr sollt über mich fahren.“
sentences.l: Then the trouble began anew, and there came a coal and said “I am big enough, I will lay myself over it and you shall drive over me.”
sentences.i: Then the trouble began all over again; and a coal came and said: “I am big enough — I will lay myself across, and you shall drive over me.”
sentences.n: Noth = modern Not, distress, trouble. angehen (to begin) is separable: “gieng… an”.

sentences.t: Die Kohle legte sich auch an das Wasser, aber sie berührte es unglücklicher Weise ein wenig, da zischte sie, verlöschte und war todt.
sentences.l: The coal did lay itself at the water, but it touched it a little, unluckily; then it hissed, went out and was dead.
sentences.i: The coal did lay itself down at the water; but unluckily it touched the water a little, and then it hissed, went out, and was dead.
sentences.n: “unglücklicher Weise” is printed as two words here (modern unglücklicherweise). Note that a coal which goes out is “todt”: the tale gives death to everything it names, straw and coal and stone alike.

sentences.t: Wie das ein Stein sah, erbarmte er sich und wollte dem Hähnchen helfen, und legte sich über das Wasser.
sentences.l: When a stone saw that, it took pity and wanted to help the little cock, and laid itself over the water.
sentences.i: When a stone saw this, he took pity and wished to help the little cock, and laid himself across the water.
sentences.n: Stein is masculine and Kohle feminine, so er and sie here are only grammar — though the tale treats them as characters anyway. “sich erbarmen” = to take pity.

sentences.t: Da zog nun das Hähnchen den Wagen selber, wie es ihn aber bald drüben hatte, und war mit dem todten Hühnchen auf dem Land und wollte die andern, die hinten auf saßen, auch heran ziehen, da waren ihrer zu viel geworden, und der Wagen fiel zurück, und alles fiel mit einander in das Wasser und ertrank.
sentences.l: Then the little cock drew the cart itself; but when it soon had it over on the other side, and was with the dead little hen on the land, and wanted to draw the others too, who sat on behind — then there had become too many of them, and the cart fell back, and everything fell in together into the water and drowned.
sentences.i: Then the little cock drew the cart himself; but just as he had it across, and stood with the dead little hen on dry land, and wanted to pull over the others who were sitting behind as well — by then there were too many of them, and the cart fell back, and everything went into the water together and drowned.
sentences.n: “ihrer zu viel” is a genitive: “too many of them”. The whole catastrophe is tucked inside a subordinate clause in one long breath, which is how this tale keeps killing without ever raising its voice.

sentences.t: Da war das Hähnchen noch allein mit dem todten Hühnchen, und grub ihm ein Grab und legte es hinein, und machte einen Hügel darüber, auf den setzte es sich und grämte sich so lang bis es auch starb; und da war alles todt.
sentences.l: Then the little cock was still alone with the dead little hen, and dug it a grave and laid it in, and made a mound over it; onto that it seated itself and grieved so long until it too died; and then everything was dead.
sentences.i: Then the little cock was left alone with the dead little hen, and dug her a grave and laid her in it, and raised a mound over her; and on the mound he sat himself down and grieved until he too died — and then everything was dead.
sentences.n: “grub ihm ein Grab” — the dative ihm is “for her”. The tale ends on one of the flattest lines in the collection, “und da war alles todt”: nothing is redeemed and nothing is explained.
